messages.subject: Shiny for twitter data --- and other examples
messages.subject_clean: Shiny for twitter data --- and other examples
messages.body_plain:
I'm new to shiny, ggplot2, and the whole R works and I've been blown away by this family of tools since I came across them a few months ago; I'm struggling to keep pace with so much to learn. Recently, I was collecting tweets for some simple text-mining apps (using shiny), and realized that it took some time in creating graphics like a word cloud. How has the experience of users been and how can the speed be increased? Since I'm not a programmer, my code is most certainly inefficient, but I am learning a lot by looking at the program documentation and code others have used in developing their apps. Is there a database of sorts or listing of different uses of shiny and perhaps,all the code used for those apps?

My first attempt at using twitter data (used in an offline manner) with shiny: http://analyticsandvisualization.blogspot.com/2013/06/tweetanalytics-interactively-analyzing.html
A couple of previous experiences with shiny (code is really ugly, so not presented; I can share them with anyone if they needed them):
1. Regarding the recently released medicare charge data - analysis focused on Spokane, where I live: http://analyticsandvisualization.blogspot.com/2013/05/medicare-provider-charge-data-how-are.html
2. Regarding different cities that were ranked by Bloomberg Businessweek as the 50 best cities in the US: http://analyticsandvisualization.blogspot.com/2013/04/interacting-on-demand-with-2012-best.html

Thanks,
Vivek

messages.subject: Installing older version of devtools in R 2.15 (on glimmer/spark)
messages.subject_clean: Installing older version of devtools in R 2.15 (on glimmer/spark)
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone -

This has been coming up on this list and off the list, so I thought I'd post this again so that it it's easy to find.

Our beta hosting servers, glimmer and spark, run R 2.15.3. However, the lastest version of devtools,1.2, requires R 3.0. To install the a version of devtools (1.1) that works with R 2.15.3, you can do the following:

download.file('http://cran.rstudio.com/src/contrib/Archive/devtools/devtools_1.1.tar.gz',
  destfile='devtools_1.1.tar.gz')
install.packages('devtools_1.1.tar.gz', type='source', repos=NULL)
unlink('devtools_1.1.tar.gz')

The next version of devtools should roll back the R version requirement; even though devtools 1.2 lists R 3.0 as a version requirement, the code appears to be compatible with R 2.15.3 as well. So hopefully in the future this won't be necessary anymore.

-Winston

> Hi Michael, great questions.
>
> On Fri, May 24, 2013 at 8:50 AM, Michael Sevast <michael...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > 1) Is concurrency limitation an issue with the beta of Shiny, or is this a limitation with R in general?
> >          If Shiny, will the upcoming commercial version address this?
>
> The issue is that R does not support concurrent execution. We plan to address this in the commercial version of Shiny by launching multiple R processes, up to 1 per user.
>
> > 2) What are the differences between the beta today and the upcoming commercial version?  is there a link to see the upcoming features and/or history of the releases?
>
> There isn't a public feature list. We intend to release a very early version of the commercial server in late June with simple authentication features, multiple R processes per app, and removal of the requirement to run the server as root. (That last feature will be upstreamed to the open source version as well.) Additional features will be in the final 1.0 release, mostly around security, monitoring, and scaling.
>
> > 3) Once the commercial version is available, what will it cost and what will the support model look like?
>
> We don't intend to charge for the preview version. Pricing for the final version and support are both TBD. If you want to contact me off-list I'd be very interested to hear what your needs and budget are.

messages.subject: Re: Set location to save .csv files and graphs?
messages.subject_clean: Set location to save .csv files and graphs?
messages.body_plain:
You can just give the file argument a full path--it doesn't have to be a bare filename. And you can use file.path to construct the full path.

Also, you want the saved_tables observer to be defined *outside* of the reactive, otherwise multiple observers will be created that all do the same thing.

Something like this:

Data <- reactive({
  # ...

  list(ID = ID, summary = data_summary, minutedata = minute_averages, hourdata = hour_averages)

})

observe({
  dir <- '/foo/bar'  # wherever you want the files to end up
  write.csv(Data()$data_summary, file = file.path(dir, "Data_summary.csv"), sep = ",")
  write.csv(Data()$minute_averages, file = file.path(dir, "Data_Minute_Averages.csv"), sep = ",")
  write.csv(Data()$hour_averages, file = file.path(dir, "Data_Hour_Averages.csv"), sep = ",")

messages.subject: passing attributes to the server
messages.body_plain:
I have a newbie question about passing data from between ui and server.

At the start of the ui.R file, I generate a named list based on a query to a data base.
The named list consists of station numbers and their names. This is then used in
a selectInput() function and the selected station number is passed to server.R as input$station

In server.R another call to the data base is made, and the resulting data plotted.

When I wanted to make the figure caption I planned to use the station name associated with
input$station. In the original list this is stored as the attribute corresponding to the station number.

However I noticed that in server.R the attribute to input$station is lost, i.e  the variable input$station
only contains the the value, but not the attribute.

What is the simplest way to pass the attribute along with the station number?

Sincerely
Halldór

The relevant bit of shiny-R code is reproduced below:

in ui.R

# Make named station list
mylist=stationPairs(SQLquery("select station_number,station_name from TABLE where CONDITIONS"))

# Define UI
shinyUI(pageWithSidebar(
...

  # Sidebar for menus and sliders
  sidebarPanel(
    selectInput("station", "Station:",choices = mylist),
...
......some further items to select.

# in server.R
df=SQLquery(paste("select time",input$item, " from TABLE where stod=",input$station," where CONDITIONS")

messages.subject: Re: rgl not working for RStudio server
messages.subject_clean: rgl not working for RStudio server
messages.body_plain:
Hi Jules,

I'm not sure whether you're referencing Shiny or the RStudio Server. If you're trying to get rgl going in Shiny, I have a guide here: http://trestletechnology.net/2013/02/graphical-tools-rgl-on-a-headless-shiny-server/. If you're working on RStudio Server, I'm not sure how to help, but I wouldn't be optimistic about an interactive rgl model working remotely -- rgl relies on OpenGL which typically is just run on the local server.

The above guide I posted is taking advantage of RGL's ability to export a model to WebGL, which makes it accessible from a browser.

Jeff

Server.r

messages.subject: Re: interactive plots?
messages.body_plain:
Is there any desire to create an archive (or tutorials) of such packages/functions, to ease the search? It would be nice to have a catalog of sorts to answer, "I am going to add a heatmap, let's look at the list to see if anyone has made something cool for heatmaps yet!", or "What types of interactive line graphs are out there?"  As is, it feels like I have to get lucky to stumble upon a thread in which people are talking about it or in a google search. So I don't know what bases are already covered or if someone is planning on adding something in particular.  Most of the ones I have found seem pretty niche, pageable from googleVis seems to be the most broadly adaptable as a replacement for generic table output. There's also the "that's cool, but I have no idea of how they got their data in the format needed to use this" factor which has come up as well.

Just wishful thinking, is all.

messages.subject: Re: Set location to save .csv files and graphs?
messages.subject_clean: Set location to save .csv files and graphs?
messages.body_plain:
Hi - update, I've come up with a solution that works with directory names entered on a Mac, but I doubt it will be platform-independent. If anyone has ideas on how to make this work for both Mac and Windows, I would be very appreciative!

#### ui.R ####

shinyUI(pageWithSidebar(
  sidebarPanel(
        textInput("dir", "Paste the filepath to the location where you would like to save the output"),   # user enters the filepath to desired folder here
        ),
         # etc.

#### server.R ####

shinyServer(function(input, output) {

  Data <- reactive({

    dir <- input$dir

     # data processing, etc.

     info <- list(dir = dir, ID = ID, summary = summary, minutedata = minute.average, hourdata = hour.average)
    return(info)
)}

 observe({
      dir <- if (is.null(Data()$dir)) { dir <- getwd() } else dir <- Data()$dir             # this line seems to keep the code from stopping due to initial lack of "dir" name

      write.csv(Data()$summary, file = file.path(dir, paste(Data()$ID,"_Data_Summary.csv", sep = "")), row.names = F)    # files are saved to folder specified in input$dir
      write.csv(Data()$minutedata, file = file.path(dir, paste(Data()$ID, "_Data_Minute_Averages.csv", sep = "")), row.names = F)
      write.csv(Data()$hourdata, file = file.path(dir, paste(Data()$ID,"_Data_Hour_Averages.csv", sep = "")), row.names=F)
    })

})

messages.body_plain:
Hi - the scenario is that the shiny app that I'm writing is for a collaborative project between researchers in New York and Ghana. The data is being collected in Ghana and the app is to enable the Ghana field staff to easily clean and process the raw data files, saving cleaned output files and plots to a location (currently in a shared Dropbox folder) that is accessible to the entire research team. There will be many, many files generated, so I would like the staff to be able to organize them within folders (most likely one folder for the output from each raw data file). Saving them to the working directory (location of the shiny app files) is not a good solution as I'd like to keep that directory pristine. At the least, I'd like to be able to specify a particular location in the Dropbox folder where the output files will be saved, but have the user able to point to this location from his/her own specific computer.

messages.subject: invalidateYield
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

  I'm thinking about enabling asynchrony in shiny in a couple ways.

  1) asynchronous URL fetches.  I have a half finished implementation for this
  2) lazy lists in R

  For the second, I need to be able to indicate that a reactive, which is otherwise invalidated, should NOT re-evaluate until after all pending writes are sent to the client.

  Otherwise, it's not going to have the interactive asynchronous property I need.

  This would work like invalidateLater(10):

  invalidateYield()

  It would not in itself invalidate the reactive, but it would force any pending invalidation to defer until after all current data was sent to the client.

-Alex

messages.subject: Re: reactive value invalidation
messages.body_plain:
On a reactive values object, the `$<-` operator is what causes invalidation. (<<- is not needed.) The invalidation only happens if the new value is different than the previous value.

K$y$S(3) would not cause an invalidation. There's no magic here. (K$y$S <- 3 would cause an invalidation, if K$y is a list or vector; and not if it's an environment or reference class object.)

messages.subject: Re: isolate(output$value <- x)
messages.body_plain:
You don't need isolate to write to a reactive value. However, output$value <- x won't work because the value you assign to an output must be a function. "output$name <- func" actually resolves down to something like this (pseudocode):

defineOutput <- function(name, func) {
  observe({
    result <- func()
    sendOutputToBrowser(name, func)
  })
}

You could do something like this though:

v <- reactiveValues(list(a=NULL))

output$value <- reactive(v$a)
(or almost-equivalently, "output$value <- function() v$a", but I think reactive(v$a) reads better at the expense of efficiency)

Then assign v$a to change the value.

Here is one way to do what Joe suggested. Suppose all your common css files are in a folder named 'common', and the absolute path to it is given by path_to_common.

addResourcePath('common', path_to_common)
tags$head(
         tags$link(rel = 'stylesheet', type = 'text/css', href = 'common/styles.css'),
         tags$link(rel = 'stylesheet', type = 'text/css', href = 'common/appStyles.css'),
)

The first line tells Shiny to map all assets starting with the prefix "common" to the full path.

Hope this helps.

messages.subject: Re: Dynamically changing plot height?
messages.body_plain:
You don't need to use renderUI for this case, instead use the renderPlot method's height argument and pass it a function, not a number. The function will be evaluated reactively and the return value is expected to be a number, which will be used as the height of the plot in pixels. The only other thing you need to do is pass height="auto" to plotOutput (since the height is going to be determined by the renderPlot height function).

I believe this is documented somewhat in ?renderPlot.

messages.subject: Re: isolate problems
messages.body_plain:
I think you need to put it in observe() instead of reactive(), or you
need to call send_query() from a reactive endpoint. If you have a
reactive expression that isn't used by any reactive endpoints, it
won't be called. You can test this by putting a print statement in
there.

A reactive endpoint is something that's in observe(). Additionally, if
you assign a reactive expression to an output, as in `output$foo <-
reactive( ... )`, it gets wrapped into an observe() under the hood.

This explained in more depth at
http://rstudio.github.io/shiny/tutorial/#reactivity-overview

-Winston

There are two options here: You can either use dynamic UI to replace
the item, or you can use conditionalPanel to hide the item.

For an example of dynamic UI, see here:
  http://glimmer.rstudio.com/winston/dynamic_ui/

For an example of conditionalPanel, see the example on the main Shiny
page. If you check "Show density estimate", a slider appears at the
bottom:
  http://www.rstudio.com/shiny/

> 2)when the user gets the new questions the radiobuttons should be reactively
> some kind of reseted.

In the new (0.6.0) version of Shiny, you can set the value of
radioButtons with updateRadioButtons(). The help page for that
function has an example of how to use it.

-Winston

Just need to remove the first "function()" (as renderPlot takes an expression, not a function); and then remove the () from assetheight (as the height parameter is a function, not an expression).

    output$riskretPlot <- renderPlot({
      makeAssetPlot()
    }, height=assetheight, width=800)

It is a little inconsistent, I know.

I created assetheight() function to calculate the changing height of the plot, but currently it says it cannot execute because it is not inside a reactive function.  I have tried moving the height function around, but without any luck. How would I modify the following code to be able to dynamically change the height? Thanks.
>
>
>     output$riskretPlot <- renderPlot(function(){
>       makeAssetPlot()
>     }, height=assetheight(), width=800)
>
>
>
> On Friday, June 7, 2013 2:10:42 AM UTC-5, Victor Kryukov wrote:
> > Thanks Joe, this is brilliant. For some reason I didn't look at renderPlot, just plotOutput, and yes, it is documented pretty clearly in renderPlot.
> >
> > On Thursday, June 6, 2013 8:04:00 PM UTC-7, Joe Cheng [RStudio] wrote:
> > > You don't need to use renderUI for this case, instead use the renderPlot method's height argument and pass it a function, not a number. The function will be evaluated reactively and the return value is expected to be a number, which will be used as the height of the plot in pixels. The only other thing you need to do is pass height="auto" to plotOutput (since the height is going to be determined by the renderPlot height function).

messages.body_plain:
It looks like you have a directory named '~' in your home directory, and ShinyApps is a subdirectory of that.

In Unix-land, the ~ character actually refers to your home directory, not a directory named '~', so you need to move ShinyApps to your home directory. Then you can also remove the '~' directory.

-Winston

messages.subject: Shiny 0.6.0 released
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone -

The long-promised Shiny 0.6.0 has been released and should be on your local CRAN mirror by now.
  http://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/shiny/index.html

Here's the list of changes from the NEWS file:

* `tabsetPanel()` can be directed to start with a specific tab selected.

* Fix bug where multiple file uploads with 3 or more files result in incorrect
  data.

* Add dateInput and dateRangeInput.

* `shinyServer()` now takes an optional `session` argument, which is used for
  communication with the session object.

* Add functions to update values of existing inputs on a page, instead of
  replacing them entirely.

* Allow listening on domain sockets.

* Added `actionButton()` to Shiny.

* The server can now send custom JSON messages to the client. On the client
  side, functions can be registered to handle these messages.

* Callbacks can be registered to be called at the end of a client session.

* Add ability to set priority of observers and outputs. Each priority level
  gets its own queue.

* Fix bug where the presence of a submit button would prevent sending of
  metadata until the button was clicked.

* `reactiveTimer()` and `invalidateLater()` by default no longer invalidate
  reactive objects after the client session has closed.

* Shiny apps can be run without a server.r and ui.r file.

-Winston

If the only problem is your HTML has extra R escaping in it, then it's possible to undo that escaping. unescape <- function(text) { parsed <- parse(text=text) if (length(parsed) != 1 || length(parsed[[1]]) != 1 || typeof(parsed[[1]]) != "character") stop("Invalid R literal string") as.character(parsed[[1]]) } output$msghtml <- renderText({ unescape(paste0('"', servervar$msg[["html"]], '"')) }) However it'd be much, much better not to have that extra R escaping in the strings in the first place, as this approach is quite fragile; if servervar$msg[["html"]] doesn't contain a string that is parseable by R, you'll get a parse error. I'm sure R is not inherently adding the escaping for you. R doesn't escape strings when it reads them, only when you print to the console (you can confirm this by using cat instead of print). If I were you I'd really focus in on how that escaping is getting into your data frame in the first place. Ah, that's exactly it. The data in test.msg appears to be corrupted. There are non-ASCII characters where it looks like they do not belong, for example on line 80 immediately following "http://links.insider.opentable.com/ctt?kn". In fact, all over the documented the string "?kn" is always followed by corruption of one kind or another (either non-ASCII characters, or, an ASCII character that doesn't make sense in that context). So forget the escaping, none of that has anything to do with anything at this point. Sorry but I misread your earlier e-mails, I thought the text was appearing in the Shiny app both ways, just with extra characters or whatever. Now that I see that the whole app is failing with an error, it's obvious that this is the problem. When you pass a non-ASCII string as an output to Shiny, it attempts to convert it to UTF-8 as that is the only kind of encoding that WebSockets support. Not only that, but the WebSockets standard says that if invalid UTF-8 data is encountered, then this is an error that causes the socket to be closed. The same is not true when a browser loads a webpage in the normal way, over HTTP; for better or worse, the traditional behavior is to be very tolerant of invalid stuff in HTML pages. That's why ui.R works (it is loaded like a normal webpage) but not server.R (it is communicated over websocket). You could fix this by processing your HTML string to strip out the invalid characters. But a better question, again, would be how those characters are getting in there in the first place. On Fri, Jun 7, 2013 at 1:30 PM, David McGarry wrote: > Thanks for the tip! messages.subject_clean: Prefetch data from web API in separate tabs
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I asked a similar question a while back: https://groups.google.com/forum/?fromgroups#!searchin/shiny-discuss/tab$20data/shiny-discuss/pEogZmy-FSw/gO2l02iiH3UJ.

I have an app (app: http://glimmer.rstudio.com/ropensci/usgs_app_sandbox/, code: https://github.com/ropensci/usgs_app/tree/ramnath) that pulls data from various web APIs for each tab based on user input in the sidebar. If the input in the sidebar is updated, new API calls are made.

My question is, What is the fastest way to prepare data on server side in all tabs (beyond just the one user is focused on)?  It seems that when going to a new tab in my app all the work has to be done to get the data for that tab. Could this work be done in the background so that when someone hits a tab the data will be ready, without slowing down the app overall?

I'm using Shiny v.0.6 in R 3.01 patched on OSX.

Thanks! Scott

That's why ui.R works (it is loaded like a normal webpage) but not server.R (it is communicated over websocket). > > You could fix this by processing your HTML string to strip out the invalid characters. If you know of workaround to be able to display these messages directly from ui.R (for example simply passing a an index from server.R to ui.R that can be used to call-up the desired msg) that would be much appreciated, but even if I can't use Shiny for this purpose it's great knowing why it isn't working (and Shiny has worked great for me when dealing with more traditional and cleaner data). Thanks again! On Fri, Jun 7, 2013 at 5:06 PM, David McGarry wrote: > Thanks Joe that does make sense. I'll see if I can trip the characters out, but do you have any idea why they display without issues when directly referenced from the ui.R? I certainly don't understand the backend of how Shiny works, but that just really confuses me. > > > On Fri, Jun 7, 2013 at 3:04 PM, Joe Cheng wrote: > > Ah, that's exactly it. The data in test.msg appears to be corrupted. There are non-ASCII characters where it looks like they do not belong, for example on line 80 immediately following "http://links.insider.opentable.com/ctt?kn". In fact, all over the documented the string "?kn" is always followed by corruption of one kind or another (either non-ASCII characters, or, an ASCII character that doesn't make sense in that context). > > > > So forget the escaping, none of that has anything to do with anything at this point. Sorry but I misread your earlier e-mails, I thought the text was appearing in the Shiny app both ways, just with extra characters or whatever. Now that I see that the whole app is failing with an error, it's obvious that this is the problem. > > > > When you pass a non-ASCII string as an output to Shiny, it attempts to convert it to UTF-8 as that is the only kind of encoding that WebSockets support. Not only that, but the WebSockets standard says that if invalid UTF-8 data is encountered, then this is an error that causes the socket to be closed. > > > > The same is not true when a browser loads a webpage in the normal way, over HTTP; for better or worse, the traditional behavior is to be very tolerant of invalid stuff in HTML pages. That's why ui.R works (it is loaded like a normal webpage) but not server.R (it is communicated over websocket). > > > > You could fix this by processing your HTML string to strip out the invalid characters. But a better question, again, would be how those characters are getting in there in the first place. > > > > > > On Fri, Jun 7, 2013 at 1:30 PM, David McGarry wrote: > > > Thanks for the tip! Sorry for the spam of messages, but just wanted to let you know that the problem was definitely with encoding. I just ran the messages through some encoding to fix it up and everything appears to be working right now. Thanks again for all of your help! On Fri, Jun 7, 2013 at 5:14 PM, David McGarry wrote: > I'm sorry, I've had a long day... I just re-read your message and now understand your section about why it loads from ui.R. Thanks for all of your help. If you know of workaround to be able to display these messages directly from ui.R (for example simply passing a an index from server.R to ui.R that can be used to call-up the desired msg) that would be much appreciated, but even if I can't use Shiny for this purpose it's great knowing why it isn't working (and Shiny has worked great for me when dealing with more traditional and cleaner data). > > Thanks again! > > On Fri, Jun 7, 2013 at 5:06 PM, David McGarry wrote: > > Thanks Joe that does make sense. I'll see if I can trip the characters out, but do you have any idea why they display without issues when directly referenced from the ui.R? I certainly don't understand the backend of how Shiny works, but that just really confuses me. > > > > > > On Fri, Jun 7, 2013 at 3:04 PM, Joe Cheng wrote: > > > Ah, that's exactly it. The data in test.msg appears to be corrupted. There are non-ASCII characters where it looks like they do not belong, for example on line 80 immediately following "http://links.insider.opentable.com/ctt?kn". In fact, all over the documented the string "?kn" is always followed by corruption of one kind or another (either non-ASCII characters, or, an ASCII character that doesn't make sense in that context). > > > > > > So forget the escaping, none of that has anything to do with anything at this point. Sorry but I misread your earlier e-mails, I thought the text was appearing in the Shiny app both ways, just with extra characters or whatever. Now that I see that the whole app is failing with an error, it's obvious that this is the problem. > > > > > > When you pass a non-ASCII string as an output to Shiny, it attempts to convert it to UTF-8 as that is the only kind of encoding that WebSockets support. Not only that, but the WebSockets standard says that if invalid UTF-8 data is encountered, then this is an error that causes the socket to be closed. > > > > > > The same is not true when a browser loads a webpage in the normal way, over HTTP; for better or worse, the traditional behavior is to be very tolerant of invalid stuff in HTML pages. That's why ui.R works (it is loaded like a normal webpage) but not server.R (it is communicated over websocket). > > > > > > You could fix this by processing your HTML string to strip out the invalid characters. But a better question, again, would be how those characters are getting in there in the first place. > > > > > > > > > On Fri, Jun 7, 2013 at 1:30 PM, David McGarry wrote: > > > > Thanks for the tip! messages.subject: R & CGI
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I want to use R to solve the classic diet linear programming problem
on a web page. The diet problem solves the problem of calculating
the amounts of a list of foods required to meet a set of constraints
at minimum cost.

To do this the code needs to process a POST statement from an existing
form and read from a MySQL database. Then it needs to use a linear
programming library, likely linprog, to find the solution, and finally
it needs to create a web page showing the solution.

Would Shiny be a good tool for this? Are there other packages, e.g.,
CGIwithR, that are more suitable?

Any suggestions, pointers, etc much appreciated.

Thanks,

BTW, the nutrient calculator, but without a linear programming solver
is online here:

http://www.nosyntax.net/birdnutrit/

-rex
--
If ingorance is bliss, why aren't more people happy?

On Fri, Jun 7, 2013 at 4:44 PM, David McGarry wrote: > Sorry for the spam of messages, but just wanted to let you know that the problem was definitely with encoding. I just ran the messages through some encoding to fix it up and everything appears to be working right now. Thanks again for all of your help! > > > On Fri, Jun 7, 2013 at 5:14 PM, David McGarry wrote: > > I'm sorry, I've had a long day... I just re-read your message and now understand your section about why it loads from ui.R. Thanks for all of your help. If you know of workaround to be able to display these messages directly from ui.R (for example simply passing a an index from server.R to ui.R that can be used to call-up the desired msg) that would be much appreciated, but even if I can't use Shiny for this purpose it's great knowing why it isn't working (and Shiny has worked great for me when dealing with more traditional and cleaner data). > > > > Thanks again! > > > > On Fri, Jun 7, 2013 at 5:06 PM, David McGarry wrote: > > > Thanks Joe that does make sense. I'll see if I can trip the characters out, but do you have any idea why they display without issues when directly referenced from the ui.R? I certainly don't understand the backend of how Shiny works, but that just really confuses me. > > > > > > > > > On Fri, Jun 7, 2013 at 3:04 PM, Joe Cheng wrote: > > > > Ah, that's exactly it. The data in test.msg appears to be corrupted. There are non-ASCII characters where it looks like they do not belong, for example on line 80 immediately following "http://links.insider.opentable.com/ctt?kn". In fact, all over the documented the string "?kn" is always followed by corruption of one kind or another (either non-ASCII characters, or, an ASCII character that doesn't make sense in that context). > > > > > > > > So forget the escaping, none of that has anything to do with anything at this point. Sorry but I misread your earlier e-mails, I thought the text was appearing in the Shiny app both ways, just with extra characters or whatever. Now that I see that the whole app is failing with an error, it's obvious that this is the problem. > > > > > > > > When you pass a non-ASCII string as an output to Shiny, it attempts to convert it to UTF-8 as that is the only kind of encoding that WebSockets support. Not only that, but the WebSockets standard says that if invalid UTF-8 data is encountered, then this is an error that causes the socket to be closed. > > > > > > > > The same is not true when a browser loads a webpage in the normal way, over HTTP; for better or worse, the traditional behavior is to be very tolerant of invalid stuff in HTML pages. That's why ui.R works (it is loaded like a normal webpage) but not server.R (it is communicated over websocket). > > > > > > > > You could fix this by processing your HTML string to strip out the invalid characters. But a better question, again, would be how those characters are getting in there in the first place. > > > > > > > > > > > > On Fri, Jun 7, 2013 at 1:30 PM, David McGarry wrote: > > > > > Thanks for the tip! messages.subject: Re: Question - help on difference between local server and online server provided by R-studio
messages.subject_clean: Question - help on difference between local server and online server provided by R-studio
messages.body_plain:
You can put this code in a new file called global.R in the same directory as ui.R and server.R. Any code in global.R gets executed before ui.R and server.R, and it executes in the global environment so any variables/functions you define are accessible anywhere.

The one caveat to using global.R is that Shiny will not notice that it has changed and re-execute it, the way that ui.R and server.R do. That means that when running locally, if you make changes to global.R you'll need to stop and re-run runApp for the changes to take effect.

When running on Glimmer (or any other Shiny Server) you can't re-run runApp, so instead, if you change the last-modified-date of a file called restart.txt in your app directory, that will instruct Shiny Server to restart the app next time. (One easy way to do this is to log onto our RStudio Server and run the command system("touch restart.txt").)

messages.subject: bitbucket: very similar repos, different behaviour
messages.subject_clean: bitbucket: very similar repos, different behaviour
messages.body_plain:
Hi -

This might be an embarrassing mistake, but I've been thrashing around with it, have a minimal example of two public repos, and I just can't see why one exports functions and the other does not.

Both load fine on my windows 7 machine.
Both load fine on shiny server, no errors
One exports no functions on shiny server

They have identical NAMESPACE (exportPattern("*.")) and identical DESCRIPTION apart from Package:, same ./R/files, both hosted on bitbucket.

If I do the following test on my windows/R2.15.2 machine, all is well - both print the function.  The problem occurs on the shiny server spark.studio.com <http://spark.studio.com>.

Thanks

Giles

#example----
require(devtools) #installed like winston said

#ex1: works fine
install_bitbucket("test","amberalpha")  #public repo
require(test)
print(buice)
detach("package:test", unload=TRUE)
remove.packages("test")

#ex2: errors
install_bitbucket("aa0","amberalpha")
require(aa0)
print(buice)    #error
detach("package:aa0", unload=TRUE)
remove.packages("aa0")

messages.body_plain:
For the deferred URL stuff I'm doing, it would be really convenient if I could use the following structure:

f <-
function(a,op2=`(`) {
  x<-op1(a)
  y<-op2(x)
     op3(y)
}

called as f(X)

Where Y could be replaced with a function meaning yield with continuation, to create the following call semanics:

z<-catch(f(X,YIELD))
... do something ...
z$continue(newOperation(z$args))

YIELD passes control immediately out of f (and any containing functions) and returns a list of continue, args, where continue is the continuation after evaluation of op2, and args is the argument to op2 (and hence yield)

calling z$continue(z$args)is thus equivalent to the function

y<-z$args
function(y)op3(y)

With the environment of f.  and z$args is set to list(x=<whatever>).  The effect of calling z$continue(z$args)

I suspect R just doesn't do this, so It's a reach, but I'm having to build horrible function chains do op3 at the moment.

-Alex

messages.body_plain:
Dear Shiny, I am extremely impressed by the package and am spending a lot of time reading over the tutorials and whatever help files I can find.  I have a question which has probably been answered a dozen times but I am afraid I need to make it again.

I would like to move linearly through a list of data sets with each click of the user's button pushing the list one item further.

I know I can do this with various other selectors such as sliders and drop boxes but I would like the progression to be linear and one way more like a slideshow that is out of the hands of the user.

The user clicks the action button and it moves forward.  I can do this of course with globals but that means that any user can push the counter forward.  I figure this is just a matter of targeting the right environment as far as modifying variables within it but I have been having difficulty doing that.

My UI code is:
actionButton("next", "Next!"),
h5(textOutput("clicks"))

My server:

clicks <- 0
  shinyServer(function(input, output) {
    output$clicks <- renderText({
      input$goButton
      eval.parent(clicks <- clicks+1)
  })
}

PS: Is there a list somewhere of all of the visitor values that are currently available to the server such as user IP?

Thanks so much!
Francis

messages.body_plain:
It looks like your description is the reverse of your code; in the code, the numericInput is xval, and the slider is power. I'll assume the code is correct.

library(shiny)

# Define server logic for slider examples
shinyServer(function(input, output) {

  xval <- reactive({
    # Take a dependency on input$powerSet by reading it. (We don't actually
    # do anything with the value.)
    # Whenever powerSet changes, this reactive expression will invalidate.
    input$powerSet

    # The actual value of xval will depend on input$xval. But since we're
    # reading it using `isolate`, input$xval changing will not automatically
    # invalidate our reactive expression.
    isolate(input$xval)
  })

  # Reactive expression to compose a data frame containing all of the values
  sliderValues <- reactive({

    input$powerSet
    # Compose data frame
    data.frame(xval()^input$power)

  })

  # Show the values using an HTML table
  output$values <- renderTable({
    sliderValues()
  })
})

messages.subject: Re: R & CGI
messages.body_plain:
Yes, Shiny would be great for this, although you'll need to move away from thinking in terms of POSTs and creating a web page with the solution. Instead, you create a ui.R file that contains areas for both the input and output, and when the inputs change (or alternatively, when the user hits a button in the UI) then the outputs will be populated with the answer. The calculations for the outputs are made in server.R.

You should start with the tutorial <http://rstudio.github.io/shiny/tutorial>, at least make your way through the first few chapters (they're quick) to get a sense of how Shiny works.

messages.body_plain:
You just have to have whatever database installed that you are using. Are you using Rstudio's glimmer? They already head sqlite3 installed, so I just had to upload my database file, and call the database from the path where it was saved on the server. It's quite simple.

I guess calling a database from a different server would require something different.

Scott

messages.subject: runApp with a List + includeHTML
messages.body_plain:
I am trying to get runApp with a list argument working along with includeHTML.

Here is a strawman app as ui.R and server.R, which works. It does not matter what the contents of www/test.html are.

# ui.R
require(shiny)
shinyUI(
  includeHTML('www/test.html')
)

# server.R
require(shiny)
shinyServer(function(input, output){

})

Now, when I tried to use the latest feature of Shiny that allows me to pass a list of ui and server to runApp, I get an error. Here is the call.

runApp(list(
  ui = includeHTML('www/test.html'),
  server = function(input, output){

  }
))

and the error I get is

Error in dependsOnFile(path) :
  addFileDependency was called at an unexpected time (no cache context found)

I know it has something to do with the includeHTML, but was unable to figure out the error.

Presently there's no way to disable Cairo output if the package is installed, but that's definitely something that would be useful -- you're not the first person to mention that Cairo output can, in some cases, look worse than regular png output.

  output$network <- renderPlot({
        browser()

        length(keep)

messages.subject: Further Developments on Shiny Dashboarding
messages.body_plain:
I wanted to share the work I've been doing extending Winston Chang's initial work with Dashboards in Shiny. I forked his initial code and have been able to flush out some of the code and create a few new widgets, as well.

You can see an example online here:
http://spark.rstudio.com/trestletech/ShinyDash-Sample/

Features include:
 - Gridster integration allows for interactive drag-and-drop functionality on flexibly sized widgets.
 - Rickshaw integration for live line and area plots with multiple series, and interactive hover/legend abilities
 - JustGage integration to provide support for animated gauges.
 - Weather widget
 - Custom HTML output widgets which can display any text/numeric values
 - A concept of "State" on each widget which can control their presentation (warning, error, etc.)

The source code behind the example is available on GitHub:
https://github.com/trestletech/ShinyDash-Sample

If you're interested in following the development of the package itself, you can do so here:
https://github.com/trestletech/ShinyDash

I'm all ears if you have any suggestions on new widgets or additional capabilities that you would find useful in this package.

messages.body_plain:
Here's an example app that's similar to what you supplied (requires Shiny 0.6.0):

runApp(list(
  ui = pageWithSidebar(
    headerPanel(""),
    sidebarPanel(
      sliderInput("slider", "Slider:",
                  min = 0, max = 1000, value = 500)
    ),
    mainPanel(
      htmlOutput("b"),
      htmlOutput("c")
    )
  ),
  server = function(input, output) {
    output$b <- renderText({
      x <- input$slider

      output$c <- renderText({ paste("output C", x) })

      paste("output B", x)
    })
  }
))

It'll work, printing out the value of input$slider for both output$b and output$c. The bad thing about it is that, output$c doesn't just re-execute every time input$slider changes -- output$c actually gets replaced (and executed) every time input$slider changes.

So, it'll work, but it doesn't really make the best use of the reactive programming model.

-Winston

messages.body_plain:
Actually, this is a better illustration of the issue:

runApp(list(
  ui = pageWithSidebar(
    headerPanel(""),
    sidebarPanel(
      sliderInput("slider", "Slider:",
                  min = 0, max = 1000, value = 500)
    ),
    mainPanel(
      htmlOutput("b"),
      htmlOutput("c")
    )
  ),
  server = function(input, output) {
    output$b <- renderText({

      output$c <- renderText({
        isolate(paste("output C", input$slider))
      })

      paste("output B", input$slider)
    })
  }
))

In this case, output$c uses isolate() around input$slider. But still, the text for c changes every time you change the slider. Compare to the usual structure, where they're not nested:

  server = function(input, output) {
    output$b <- renderText({

      paste("output B", input$slider)
    })
    output$c <- renderText({
      isolate(paste("output C", input$slider))
    })
  }

In this case, output$c doesn't change in response to the slider.

-Winston

messages.body_plain:
I have solved my question reading this comment (link:https://gist.github.com/jcheng5/4050398/#comment-801300)

I am adding a bit of information to this page, since it took me 20 minutes to figure out which is stupid I know, it probably will take someone else it as well.

Most people, like me, will actually want to use the file. When you upload, you do not upload the file but a group of strings, this is what you see when you use the code above. Using the 'datapath' column you are able to use the normal ways to get your data, e.g. read.csv()

Seeing the post linked below made me realize this, using the line:

inFile <- input$files

you get the uploaded data (note this does not contain the file yet) in a data.frame. If you use

dataset<-read.csv(inFile$datapath, header=T, stringsAsFactors =F)

you actually get the data you want in the variable 'dataset'. The variable inFile$datapath contains the path to the file. Now you have the data, play around with it! Using the normal code for the UI you should see your table.

Might be redundant, but since this is one of the first hits on google, I guess it won't hurt.

messages.subject: a first try Shiny app: Center for Medicare and Medicaid (CMS) 2011 DRG hospital charge/pay data
messages.subject_clean: a first try Shiny app: Center for Medicare and Medicaid (CMS) 2011 DRG hospital charge/pay data
messages.body_plain:
Thanks to the tutorial, kind responses from Winston and Joe to a REALLY basic issue about naming folders on the RStudio server, and discussion on this group, I built a simple Shiny app running on the RStudio spark server.

Display is available at http://spark.rstudio.com/iecodesign/DRG_App1/

Here is the gist   https://gist.github.com/klittle314/5784204

To reproduce the display, you need to put this CMS data file in your app directory,

http://www.cms.gov/Research-Statistics-Data-and-Systems/Statistics-Trends-and-Reports/Medicare-Provider-Charge-Data/Inpatient.html

I renamed the file CMSexample.csv from the default download name.

The app allows user to choose one of 100 DRG (Diagnostic Related Group codes, click on the cms link to learn more about the data).  Then the application subsets the master data file by the chosen DRG, further summarizes the data by state, creates a Google map via googleVis tools, creates a small multiples scatter plot array (faceted scatter plot) in ggplot2, and makes the DRG level data set available for download.

For new users like me, the code may help you see details (e.g. need to make explicit the print() command with ggplot2) and save you some time.  I learn best from examples!

I welcome comments on how to make the R code better.

Kevin Little

Hi there, I've just started using Shiny, and enjoying it so far :)

However, I have a little problem - I'm trying to use Shiny as a dashboard using the Google Analytics API.  I have had success preloading the API calls in the global.R script for fixed queries, but I now want to make the API calls respond to user's input via Shiny's ui.R.

Depending on the date ranges and the metrics/dimensions a user puts in, this could take quite a long time to query the API, especially for rollups that may involve ~200 calls to GA API.

Doing this in RStudio is fine, as the API script writes to the console, giving user feedback, but for Shiny Server I don't know how to output this info whilst a user is waiting.  This will also help debugging the board :)

Are there any tips for the above? If I could just dump what I normally see in RStudio console whilst running the functions into a reactive output that would be great (and useful anyhow for other things), or if the print calls used in the function runs could be outputted as the function runs that may be better? It would also be nice for making progress bars for any functions that will take a long time.

Yours faithfully,
Mark

Hi,

I've installed shiny-server (using Ubuntu13.04) and have been testing out some new applications I've developed via remote browser. I noticed that after multiple access, the computer started to work much slower, even freeze, requiring a re-boot. Eventually, I discovered that the system memory was gradually being consumed by multiple R-sessions that were launched during the initialization of each shiny app, and persist after the access to that app has been disconnected (at least remotely via the browser).  With multiple access, I can end up with dozens of sleeping R processes. Is this expected behaviour?

Thanks!

messages.body_plain:
Hm, this may require some modification to renderPlot. It appears that the call to png() needs to have bg="transparent".

For example:

library(ggplot2)

trans_theme <- theme(

    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major = element_blank(),

    panel.background = element_rect(fill=NA),
    plot.background = element_rect(fill=NA)
)

png("transparent.png", bg = "transparent")
qplot(1:3, 1:3) + trans_theme
dev.off()

png("white.png", bg = "white")
qplot(1:3, 1:3) + trans_theme
dev.off()

## Same behavior with CairoPNG
library(Cairo)
CairoPNG("transparent_cairopng.png", bg = "transparent")
qplot(1:3, 1:3) + trans_theme
dev.off()

CairoPNG("white_cairopng.png", bg = "white")
qplot(1:3, 1:3) + trans_theme
dev.off()

I've filed an issue about it at: https://github.com/rstudio/shiny/issues/178

-Winston

messages.subject: Re: How to create a table with reactive links
messages.subject_clean: How to create a table with reactive links
messages.body_plain:
Two options off the top of my head:

1. If the size of your table is small, you can pre-generate HTML pages and then link to them from the table. This can all be done automatically (give the page a name related to the ID in the table and then construct a link to it). messages.subject: Re: error messages in R console and blank downloaded plot
messages.subject_clean: error messages in R console and blank downloaded plot
messages.body_plain:
getplot shouldn't be a reactive, since it doesn't (can't) store and return a plot; plot() works by writing to the active plotting device at the time that it's called. So instead of getplot it should be called perhaps "doplot", and be made into a regular function instead of a reactive expression. In other words, whenever you're calling it, you want it to *actually* execute (whereas a reactive expression doesn't actually execute unless the value it already has is out of date).

That fixes #3. The other problems all stem from this line:

USArrests$state<-sn

I'm not sure what you're doing there, but it causes the warnings and the failed plot.

> >
> >
> > On 21 February 2013 00:29, floe <flo...@endel.at> wrote:
> > > The entered username can be passed to the corresponding R instance by utilizing the AppSpec Object (appSpec instance) located in lib/worker/app-spec.js .
> > > Inside the httpListener in lib/proxy/http.js (--> last post!) the following authentication code is inserted:
> > >
> > > > basic.apply(req, res, function(username) {
> > > >   router.getAppSpec_p(req, res)
> > > >   .then(function(appSpec) {
> > > >     appSpec.settings.loginName = username;
> > > >   })
> > > > });
> > >
> > > This property of appSpec has to be passed to a newly spawned R process by altering lib/worker/app-worker.js around line 150. At the end of the parameter to "this.$proc.stdin.end", where the stdin ('command line') parameters of the R process are generated, the following line is added:
> > > > (appSpec.settings.loginName || '') + '\n'
> > > (Do not forget the additional "+" in the line above.)
> > >
> > > Next the new command line parameter has to be added to the R environment. In "./R/SockJSAdapter.R" these parameters are read right at the beginning and are copied to the local R environment. Therefor the "Sys.setenv" function gets a new entry:
> > > > USERNAME=input[4]
> > > (Again do not forget to get the "," etc. right.)
> > >
> > > Finally the provided username can be used inside the shiny (R) application:
> > > > Sys.getenv('USERNAME')
> > >
> > >  Yet again be aware that this is a crude hack by a highly inexperienced user (in fact I've seen any details about node.js for the first time about 24 ago :)

> > > FloE

> > > > After the the first block of code where all the libraries are loaded I added:
> > > > > var auth = require('http-auth');
> > > > > var basic = auth({
> > > > >     authRealm : "Private area.",
> > > > >     authList : ['user1:pwd1', 'user2:pwd2']
> > > > > });
> > > >
> > > > The authentication logic is applied directly to the httpListener. Therefore after
> > > > > this.httpListener = function(req, res) {
> > > > the following line is inserted:
> > > > > basic.apply(req, res, function(username) {});
> > > >
> > > > After saving and closing the file, the server has to be restarted.

> > > > Be aware that this is a very inflexible and unsafe hack.
> > > >
> > > > I would be most interesting how the entered username can be passed to the corresponding R instance(s)?!
> > > >
> > > > Hopefully a more intelligent authentication feature will be added to future versions :)

> > > > FloE

> > > > On Friday, January 18, 2013 9:51:43 PM UTC+1, jphilip wrote:

messages.subject: Re: Feedback from Console as an reactive output? Or way to report progress
messages.subject_clean: Feedback from Console as an reactive output? Or way to report progress
messages.body_plain:
Sorry, we don't currently have a good answer for this, unless you know a little HTML/JavaScript. You can have your shinyServer function take a "session" param: (function (input, output, session) )

and then in your server.R you can make calls like this:

session$sendCustomMessage("progress", list(
  completed = completedUnits / totalUnits,
  message = progressMessage
))

In your ui.R you can inject some JavaScript that does something like this:

Shiny.addCustomMessageHandler("progress", function(data) {
  // Do something with data.completed and data.message
});

Now you have a connection between the server and the client; you could use some JavaScript to actuate a Twitter Bootstrap progress bar <http://twitter.github.io/bootstrap/components.html#progress>, for example.

(Eventually this will all get wrapped up nice in a bow for you so you don't need to do any custom JS of your own, but since progress probably needs to be pretty flexible, it's not something that we have had time to do just yet.)

messages.body_plain:
Not at all. But, when I went to that link, I immediately got a page with an angry pink unicorn on it saying "this page is taking too long to load." I'm guessing the server is out getting shave and a haircut somewhere and will be back sometime after morning tea? In the alternative, what I'd submit would be something along the lines of ... There is currently no apparent (or documented) way to access (or construct) the response object. This would be useful in being able to add, remove, or modify http headers, for instance. Although most such headers can be added by using the tag, there is at least one exception, which requires, for security reasons, that the header be added by the server proper: Access-Control-Accept-Origin. This is part of the Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (W3C) standard which allows controlled accesses to multiple different servers from within the same web page. One can do this using IFRAMEs but because these are completely isolated from their peer DOM objects those peers cannot access the IFRAME's contents. Hence, no resources can be shared this way. By allowing cross-origin access, a DIV or other, non-isolating container can be loaded (via jQuery's load method, for instance) from a site other than the one the page itself came from. Example: I have a website at http://localhost:8080/index.html looking something like: ...

This is an example of embedding shiny ala CORS

(I've left out or oversimplified a bunch of stuff, but it gives yout he general idea.) On the shiny (server) side I'll get a collection of headers that include: Origin: http://localhost:8080 So my shiny server will have to put a header in the response that looks like: Access-Control-Accept-Origin: http://localhost:8080 to allow cross-site access specifically from localhost:8080, or Access-Control-Accept-Origin: * to allow cross-site access from any host. WARNING: this can leave you vulnerable to cross-site scripting (XSS) attacks, so BEWARE! messages.subject: Re: selectInput enhancements?
messages.body_plain:
Hm, that is very slow. Here's an example app:

library(shiny)

n_choices <- 5000

runApp(list(
  ui = pageWithSidebar(
    headerPanel(""),
    sidebarPanel(
      uiOutput("ui")
    ),
    mainPanel(
      verbatimTextOutput("text")
    )
  ),
  server = function(input, output) {
    output$ui <- renderUI({
      choices <- paste0("choice", 1:n_choices)
      names(choices) <- choices

      selectInput("select", "Select:", multiple = TRUE, choices = choices)
    })

    output$text <- renderText({
      input$select
    })
  }
))

And here's code that illustrates the problem more directly:
  n_choices <- 5000
  choices <- paste0("choice", 1:n_choices)
  names(choices) <- choices
  s <- selectInput("select", "Select:", multiple = TRUE, choices = choices)

I'll look into speeding it up.

-Winston

Welcome to R!  may it be your comfy home for many years.

A great place to start is the R website:

But let me give you a quick tour.

R is a programming language (you write programs in it), a platform (which provides many useful tools to help you write programs), a community of programmers, academics, scientists and industrialists who use the R language and share programs, packages (sets of tools) and tips, and the occasional handshake.

It's best known for it's awesome package library - if you can think of a problem in the area of statistics, data processing, visualization any many more, it's probably been solved and turned into a ready made tool by someone already, and for it's sparkling graphics capabilities.  Edward Tufte, who literally *wrote the book* on data visualization, rates R as the most happening place to be for data display right now.

step right in, the water is warm.

messages.subject: Re: Google Analytics tracking code
messages.body_plain:
I didn't use any built-in GA features if there were any.  I just used tags$head(tags$script()) and put two things in it:

Track a page view.  Not so useful since shiny is ajax-like and url doesn't change.

  (function(i,s,o,g,r,a,m){i['GoogleAnalyticsObject']=r;i[r]=i[r]||function(){
        (i[r].q=i[r].q||[]).push(arguments)},i[r].l=1*new Date();a=s.createElement(o),
        m=s.getElementsByTagName(o)[0];a.async=1;a.src=g;m.parentNode.insertBefore(a,m)
        })(window,document,'script','//www.google-analytics.com/analytics.js <http://www.google-analytics.com/analytics.js>','ga');

        ga('create', 'UA-XXXXXXX-XX',...)

        ga('send', 'pageview');

Track an event (e.g., user uploads file, changes selectInput, etc)

    $(document).on('change','#client',function(evt) {
      ga('send', 'event', 'Setup', 'Set Name', $(this).val());
    });

This setup is working wonderfully for tracking what users are doing on the app.

messages.subject: Re: Problems with renderUI's reactivity
messages.body_plain:
When it executes val(), if the value changes, it will invalidate its descendants, namely output$textbox. However, if the returned value of val() doesn't change, then it won't invalidate them.

-Winston

On Tue, Jun 18, 2013 at 5:32 AM, Peter <peter.will...@gmail.com> wrote:

> I am trying to understand why "# Option 1" in server.R doesn't work, but commented "# Option 2" does work. With "# Option 1" being active try typing random string and pressing the button. First time it replaces the values in the textbox with "abc", but all the next times doesn't.
>
> In my understanding val() is already dependent on input$change, so it must re-execute every time the button is pressed, furthermore "# Option 2" is wrapped into  isolate(), so it doesn't add any reactivity.
>
> It seems that actually the value partially changes to "abc" when using  "# Option 1". Having Google Chrome's inspect element opened you can see that "# Option 2" changes the values of <input id="txt" type="text" ...> every time the button is pressed,  "# Option 1" also changes the value to "abc", but the the screen is updated only when the button is pressed for the first time.
>
> Here is the code:
>
> server.R
>
> shinyServer(function(input, output) {
>
>   val <- reactive({
>     if(input$change>0) {
>      # Option 1
>       'abc'
> #       # Option 2
> #       isolate({
> #         paste('abc',input$txt,"")
> #       })
>     } else {
>       ''
>     }
>   })
>
>   output$textbox <- renderUI({
>     textInput("txt","Text",val())
>   })
>
> })
>

>

>   ),
>

>
>   )
> ))

messages.subject: Re: invalidateLater with tabsetPanel
messages.body_plain:
Hi Jeff -

Outputs are suspended when they're not visible on the page. You can use the outputOptions function to change this behavior. In shinyServer() function:
  outputOptions(output, "myplot", suspendWhenHidden = FALSE)

-Winston

Is there a way to make the reactive endpoint invalidate even if it is not currently visible? Is there a difference between using invalidateLater() and reactiveTimer() that would make a difference here?

messages.body_plain:
Fun stuff- combines my love of football (go Ravens! Born and raised
Baltimorean) with shiny.  I have never actually used a cap in any of my
leagues, and I suspect a modified version could be useful for such
leagues, in a version like Joe mentioned, it would cut down the
research/decision time needed when the the guy you wanted and the backup
 selection that you had in mind just in case get nabbed the two picks
ahead of you.  Perhaps a real time suggestion list (or table with
projected stats) could be generated after each team's pick?  It may not
always be the best available player that you want to select in a given
round, if the next half a dozen players at his position aren't much
different than him, you can afford to select another player at another
position where the value may not hold up until your next selection.  How
 to calculate any of that I have no idea, I just wing it on draft day,
heh.

Does the app take the players bye weeks into consideration?  I tend to prefer players with bye weeks later in the season, for example.  Also, the dreaded suicide backup week is a good thing to avoid.

Tangent- personally I migrated my leagues from yahoo to fleaflicker, and have rather enjoyed the change.

In any event, good work, Isaac!

If I understand the question correctly... Similarly to inputs vs. reactiveValues, you can create something similar but you can't actually hook it up to the communication channel with the client. Inputs are implemented using reactiveValues which are set by shinyapp; outputs are implemented using observers that write their results to shinyapp.

All that said, I'm not sure why you would need any more than the regular input and output objects to implement what you're talking about.

messages.subject: Re: Problems with renderUI's reactivity
messages.body_plain:
Ignore what Winston said. :) val() will invalidate its callers regardless of whether the returned value changes or not.

The problem isn't in the reactivity; if you set "options(shiny.trace=TRUE)" you can see that when you click the button, the value is going to the server ("RECV"); and that the server replies back with the HTML for textbox ("SEND"). Yet nothing actually changes on the client.

The problem is that the client knows what the previous value of the output was, and since the new version is no different, it thinks it's safe to ignore it rather than having the new value rendered. I'm not sure whether I consider this a feature or a bug.

In your case I think you would want to use updateTextInput() in an observe() call, anyway...

> When it executes val(), if the value changes, it will invalidate its descendants, namely output$textbox. However, if the returned value of val() doesn't change, then it won't invalidate them.
>
> -Winston
>
>

> >
> > In my understanding val() is already dependent on input$change, so it must re-execute every time the button is pressed, furthermore "# Option 2" is wrapped into  isolate(), so it doesn't add any reactivity.
> >
> > It seems that actually the value partially changes to "abc" when using  "# Option 1". Having Google Chrome's inspect element opened you can see that "# Option 2" changes the values of <input id="txt" type="text" ...> every time the button is pressed,  "# Option 1" also changes the value to "abc", but the the screen is updated only when the button is pressed for the first time.
> >

> > server.R
> >

> >
> >   val <- reactive({
> >     if(input$change>0) {
> >      # Option 1

On Tue, Jun 18, 2013 at 2:25 PM, Joe Cheng <j...@rstudio.com> wrote:

>
> The problem is that the client knows what the previous value of the output was, and since the new version is no different, it thinks it's safe to ignore it rather than having the new value rendered. I'm not sure whether I consider this a feature or a bug.

> In your case I think you would want to use updateTextInput() in an observe() call, anyway...
>
>

messages.subject: Expand/collapse wellPanel on click. Possible?
messages.body_plain:
Is it possible to use Javascript with Shiny to expand and collapse individual wellPanels in the sidebar upon a button click? I have tried various manifestations of mixing some canned javascript with shiny apps but no luck yet.
For example, things like:

sidebarPanel(
tags$head(
tags$script(type="text/javascript", src="http://code.jquery.com/jquery-1.9.1.js") #### or: src="www/js/jquery-1.9.1.js"
                ....
        ),
        HTML("<button>Expand/Collapse</button>"),
        div(id='wpDiv1',class='wpDiv',
        wellPanel(...
                #### various input controls
                ...)
        ),...

and somewhere, but I don't know where, something like:
<script>
$("button").click(function () {
$("wpDiv").slideToggle("slow");
});
</script>

which I'll call button1.html and for the time being I have included in the sidebarPanel call as includeHTML("www/html/button1.html")

Of course, none of this works, except for the simple HTML("<button>Expand/Collapse</button>") call which does make a non-functional button. I am guessing the tags$script thing is not right. I have tried various combination of tags, div, HTML, includeHTML. I have tried the shinyIncubator actionButton instead of the generic button. I have tried different placements in the ui.R script. But I don't actually even know if this is something that is possible to do in the first place. I would like a wellPanel that begins short, only revealing say, a button, which can be clicked to expand the wellPanel to show a larger vertical list of inputs (and shrink back as well). Can this be done?

Thanks,
Matt

You can always base64 encode the images; see http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Data_URI_scheme There are a number of ways to do this in R. messages.subject: Re: Trouble writing files on shiny-server
messages.body_plain:
This is the correct default behavior; you generally want your R process to be running under a fairly restricted set of permissions, in case there is a security hole in your code (or in Shiny) an attacker won't be able to modify anything. However, if you do need to make modifications then you can change the config to allow that.

In this case, I'd create a subdirectory of your app dir (shiny_test) for the "shiny" user to write to:

# Create the directory
sudo mkdir /var/shiny-server/www/shiny_test/work
# Make shiny the owner of the directory
sudo chown shiny:shiny /var/shiny-server/www/shiny_test/work

Then change the path you pass to write.csv to be "work/time.csv" instead of "time.csv".

So, note that list in R are substantially more powerful than hash maps in other languages.

1) they are ordered and can be intreated and indexed in that order

messages.body_plain:
I have a simple Shiny app that reads a mysql table and displays a graph of aggregated data.  the app works fine on a local Mac (I use a tunnel to enable RMySQL to connect to MySql DB running on EC2)

Next step - I used Shiny AMI to spin an EC2 micro instance, put mysql on it so I am able to do tunnel through mysql socket to the real MySQL server running on another EC2 instance (same setup as on my local Mac that works)

Next step - I test that mysql connection through tunnel is working in R by running an R shell on EC micro with Shiny and running the same R commands as in my Shiny App: establish connection, do a select on a table using dbSendQuery. Everything works fine, just like on a local machine (I use Mac)

Now the fun part, I go to Shiny URL in the browser to  point to the shiny on EC2 instance.  Application starts ok and connects to MySQL (I know because when I had misconfigured tunnel it gave me error messages at this point).  However, when I try to click on something that would trigger a select it hangs for a while and then crashes.  When I go to Shiny log on the server I see the following cryptic error message:

Listening on port 51279
Warning in mysqlExecStatement(conn, statement, ...) :
  RS-DBI driver warning: (unrecognized MySQL field type 7 in column 38 imported as character)
Warning in mysqlExecStatement(conn, statement, ...) :
  RS-DBI driver warning: (unrecognized MySQL field type 7 in column 39 imported as character)
Warning in mysqlExecStatement(conn, statement, ...) :
  RS-DBI driver warning: (unrecognized MySQL field type 7 in column 1 imported as character)
Warning in mysqlExecStatement(conn, statement, ...) :
  RS-DBI driver warning: (unrecognized MySQL field type 7 in column 4 imported as character)
Error in .getReactiveEnvironment()$currentContext() :
  Operation not allowed without an active reactive context. (You tried to do something that can only be done from inside a reactive function.)
Calls: runApp ... $ -> $.reactivevalues -> <Anonymous> -> <Anonymous>
Execution halted

As you can see by the warnings it was able to do a select, however I am not sure at which point and why it crashed.  Any ideas are appreciated. This error is reproducible and occurs every time.  Table is about 10k rows so should have no memory issues

kind regards,

messages.subject: Re: Hashmap, associative arrays in R
messages.body_plain:
One drawback to lists in R is that they're copied on write, so they can be slow if you're modifying a large list in-place. (I don't know exactly which parts are copied on write -- I don't think every item is copied on write, but the references to them are copied.)

Here's an example that shows how slow it can be to modify a list in-place using a for-loop:

# Generate a bunch of names to use as keys
item_names <- paste0("item", 1:20000)

# Measure the time to evaluate the expression
system.time( {
  x <- list()
  for (name in item_names) {
    x[[name]] <- 0
  }
})
#  user  system elapsed
# 4.928   0.764   5.711

Assigning 20,000 items to a list this way takes about 5 seconds.

What about environments? Unlike lists, environments aren't copied on write, so they don't slow down when modifying them in-place:

system.time( {
  e <- new.env()
  for (name in item_names) {
    e[[name]] <- 0
  }
})
#  user  system elapsed
# 0.054   0.000   0.054

# environments don't preserve order, so they won't be identical
identical(x, as.list(e))
# [1] FALSE

You can actually generate a list in one go using lapply instead of a for loop, and this is much faster since the list isn't being modified in place (and thus being copied many times):

system.time( {
  #  Create a named vector to use as the source of the lapply
  vec <- numeric(length(item_names))
  names(vec) <- item_names

  # Generate a new list using lapply
  y <- lapply(vec, function(x) 0)
})
#  user  system elapsed
# 0.005   0.000   0.005

# Exactly the same result as the original version
identical(x, y)
# [1] TRUE

You might think, maybe it's the lapply that makes this last example really fast -- perhaps the for-loop used in the first two versions is slower than the lapply used in the third. But actually, lapply is slightly slower than a for-loop. The speed advantage of an lapply is that it collects the output into a list -- if you instead do the list assignments in a loop, it can be an expensive operation, as shown in the first example.

To illustrate: the next example uses an environment (like the second example) and it uses lapply (like the third example) but the lapply is simply being used to assign items in an environment; it's not being used to collect the output.

# Speed with lapply instead of for loop is slightly slower
system.time({
  e2 <- new.env()
  lapply(names, function(name) {
    e2[[name]] <- 0
  })
})
#  user  system elapsed
# 0.072   0.000   0.072

-Winston

> 2) they can contain a mix of named and not named data
> 3) they can contain repeated named.  The first is returned

> They have compact addressing for path accesses, but I have not used this yet

messages.subject: Re: Shiny crash on EC2 with cryptic message: "Operation not allowed without an active reactive context."
messages.subject_clean: Shiny crash on EC2 with cryptic message: "Operation not allowed without an active reactive context."
messages.body_plain:
That error happens when you access a reactive object outside of a reactive context like renderText(), reactive(), and observe(). For example, the input values are reactive. This is ok:

shinyServer(input, output) {
  output$txt <- renderText({ input$num })
}

But accessing input$num outside of the renderText() will result in that error:

shinyServer(input, output) {
  input$num
}

The same is true if you try to access a reactive expression outside of a reactive context.

-Winston

messages.subject: Re: runApp and Environment
messages.body_plain:
Hi Ramnath -

The environment is inherited from where the function is _defined_, not from where it is called. For example:

f <- function() {
  x <- 10
  g()
}

g <- function() x

# g() doesn't inherit the environment from f()
f()
# Error in g() : object 'x' not found

# Return a closure (function + env) that records x
a <- function() {
  x <- 10
  function() x
}

# Save the closure returned by a()
b <- a()

# Run the closure
b()
# [1] 10

-Winston

messages.subject: Re: Live Data
messages.body_plain:
Yes, we are about to merge a function called reactivePoll (tentative name) that will make this relatively straightforward to do. However, it will not be all that appropriate if the call to get stock quotes takes a long time, as it will hold up the R process as the request is being made.

If the call does take a long time, then another way to go would be to have a separate process running that continually looks for and downloads new data, and updates a file on disk. Then the Shiny process simply needs to check the disk for changes periodically and load when changes are detected--the same merge that has reactivePoll will also have reactiveFileReader which implements part of this.

On Wed, Jun 19, 2013 at 5:00 AM, Michael Guan <michael...@gmail.com> wrote:

> I was wondering if it possible to connect live data into shiny. Ie: stock quotes.
>
> I feel that the constant update will make the loading blurry all the time.
>
> Is this possible?
>
> Thanks

messages.subject: Re: Shiny crash on EC2 with cryptic message: "Operation not allowed without an active reactive context."
messages.subject_clean: Shiny crash on EC2 with cryptic message: "Operation not allowed without an active reactive context."
messages.body_plain:
Hi Winston,

I don't see anything like this in my code (which is very simple and shown below), in addition the same code works fine from my iMac, so unless it is a version of Shiny or EC2 issue I don't see how the same code produces this error on Linux but not on MacOS

server.R:

shinyServer(function(input, output) {

  all.objects <- read_object_data_from_db()

  lastDate <- all.objects$accounts$created[nrow(all.objects$accounts)]

  # Return the requested dataset
  datasetInput <- reactive({

    switch(input$dataset,
           "accounts" = all.objects$accounts,
           "datapoints" = all.objects$datapoints)
  })

  output$growthChart <-  renderPlot({
    n <- as.integer(input$aggDays)
    dates <- seq(from=lastDate - 7*input$lookbackWeeks, to=lastDate, by=n)

    objectCountsByDate <- data.frame(dates=dates,
                                     counts=sapply(dates, createdBefore, datasetInput()))

    p <- generateGrowthCharts(objectCountsByDate, "Accounts")
     print(p)

  })
})

On Wednesday, June 19, 2013 8:05:29 AM UTC-7, Winston Chang wrote:
> That error happens when you access a reactive object outside of a reactive context like renderText(), reactive(), and observe(). For example, the input values are reactive. This is ok:
>
> shinyServer(input, output) {
>   output$txt <- renderText({ input$num })
> }
>
>
> But accessing input$num outside of the renderText() will result in that error:
>
> shinyServer(input, output) {
>   input$num
> }
>
>
> The same is true if you try to access a reactive expression outside of a reactive context.
>
> -Winston
>
>
>
>
>
> On Wed, Jun 19, 2013 at 3:02 AM, Ilya Li <ilip...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > I have a simple Shiny app that reads a mysql table and displays a graph of aggregated data.  the app works fine on a local Mac (I use a tunnel to enable RMySQL to connect to MySql DB running on EC2)
> >
> > Next step - I used Shiny AMI to spin an EC2 micro instance, put mysql on it so I am able to do tunnel through mysql socket to the real MySQL server running on another EC2 instance (same setup as on my local Mac that works)
> >
> > Next step - I test that mysql connection through tunnel is working in R by running an R shell on EC micro with Shiny and running the same R commands as in my Shiny App: establish connection, do a select on a table using dbSendQuery. Everything works fine, just like on a local machine (I use Mac)
> >
> > Now the fun part, I go to Shiny URL in the browser to  point to the shiny on EC2 instance.  Application starts ok and connects to MySQL (I know because when I had misconfigured tunnel it gave me error messages at this point).  However, when I try to click on something that would trigger a select it hangs for a while and then crashes.  When I go to Shiny log on the server I see the following cryptic error message:
> >
> > Listening on port 51279
> > Warning in mysqlExecStatement(conn, statement, ...) :
> >   RS-DBI driver warning: (unrecognized MySQL field type 7 in column 38 imported as character)
> > Warning in mysqlExecStatement(conn, statement, ...) :
> >   RS-DBI driver warning: (unrecognized MySQL field type 7 in column 39 imported as character)

> > Calls: runApp ... $ -> $.reactivevalues -> <Anonymous> -> <Anonymous>
> > Execution halted

> >
> >
> > As you can see by the warnings it was able to do a select, however I am not sure at which point and why it crashed.  Any ideas are appreciated. This error is reproducible and occurs every time.  Table is about 10k rows so should have no memory issues
> >

messages.body_plain:
What you're describing sounds like the opposite of what Alex was asking for in this thread. I'll describe both:

1) Alex was asking to be able to specify which tab in a tabset would be selected by default; that's the "selected" parameter on tabsetPanel

2) It sounds like you're asking to know which tab is currently selected; you specify the "id" parameter on tabsetPanel and use input$foo (for example, assuming id="foo") in your server.R.

messages.body_plain:
Aye, it is a snake draft.  And I don't believe there is any consensus for best bye weeks- that's just been a little trick of mine which has helped me win a few championships ;).  But it is fairly common for people to avoid drafting a team which would result in an abundance of players on a bye week at the same time, especially WRs and RBs- and having a backup player with the same bye week as a starter- especially in the one option positions (typically QB, TE, K, DEF), is downright useless.

Thanks!
Mike

On Wednesday, June 19, 2013 7:24:30 PM UTC-4, Isaac Petersen wrote:
> Thanks for the feedback, guys.  In response to your questions/ideas:
>
> Mike, is your league a snake draft?  If so, I'm planning to write another app for snake drafts.  I'll make sure to include a table of projected points, value, and risk for various players at different positions.  This shiny app was designed for auction drafts (which have a cap).  The app doesn't take bye weeks into consideration, but it would feasible to do so.  I don't know if there is a consensus around the best bye weeks to have.
>
> Joe, that's a very interesting idea about the realtime projected points as games are played.  I'm looking forward to hearing about the upcoming Shiny features for checking for updated data sets.

messages.subject: Re: runApp + List + dependsOnFile

It is unfortunate but expected. Using runApp with an object means the UI only gets rendered once, and no file changes are detected. We may have a workaround in the future but nothing today.
